sections.h2: Where Boulder County deeds are recorded
sections.html:
The Boulder County Clerk and Recorder takes in deeds, deeds of trust, liens, plats and court documents for every property in the county. The Recording Division is at 1750 33rd St., Suite 201, in Boulder. Reach it at 303-413-7770 or recording@bouldercounty.gov.

A sale becomes part of the public record only once it is recorded. The signed deed comes to this office when a house changes hands, and the buyer's lender files its deed of trust in the same visit. Boulder County is about 740 square miles with Boulder as its seat. Longmont and Erie reach into Weld County, and Superior reaches into Jefferson County, so a deed for a house near those lines still goes to the county where the parcel sits.

Filing one document costs $43, a rate that began July 1, 2025, with the state documentary fee added where it applies. Checks are payable to Boulder County Clerk & Recorder.

ServiceFee
Recording, per document$43
Documentary fee$0.01 per $100 of consideration, on non-exempt deeds over $500
Certifying a copy of a recorded document$1
Non-digital copies$0.25 per page
UCC recording, 1 to 2 pages$13
UCC recording, 3 or more pages$18
E-recorded UCC$8
Recording a death certificateNo charge

For any charge not in the table, call the office at the number above.

Colorado charges one cent per $100 of consideration, starting once the price passes $500. The rule is C.R.S. 39-13-102, and collection is the county clerk and recorder's job. Your closing agent works out the figure and shows it on the settlement statement.

The base is more than the sticker price. The statute counts the price plus any lien or encumbrance and the charges paid to make the transfer. It also treats a property as residential unless the deed carries a conspicuous note that it is not. The documentary fee is the only charge tied to the price of a deed, and Colorado adds no separate transfer tax on top of it.

If a house sits in more than one county, the fee is split between the county recorders in proportion to the value in each, with the person recording the deed making the allocation.

Four routes exist: mail, a 24-hour drop box, the counter, or e-recording by a title company. Each one has limits.

  • Mail: send the Recording Division the document, a check and a return address.
  • Drop boxes: 1750 33rd St. in Boulder, 1755 S. Public Road in Lafayette, and 529 Coffman St. in Longmont. Mark the folder "Recording" and add contact details.
  • In person: the counter is open Monday through Thursday, 7:30 a.m. to 5 p.m., and closed Fridays.
  • Email: individual owners can send a scanned PDF, with extra fees. Brokerages, title companies, lenders and law firms cannot use this route.
  • E-recording: high-volume filers use Simplifile, eRecording Partners, CSC or Indecomm. This is the only option described as same-day.

Drop-offs in Lafayette or Longmont travel by interoffice mail to Boulder, which can add one to two business days. If your closing date is tight, use the Boulder box or counter.

sections.h2: What a deed needs before filing
sections.html:
A deed needs the correct fee, a return address and no personal identifying information, because recorded documents are public. Remove such details before filing.

The clerk cannot pull back a recorded document, and the staff cannot advise you on which document to file. For a house sale, a title company or attorney drafts the deed and checks the legal description. A cash buyer works the same way, with the closing agent handling the recording step.

Boulder County runs a public search site where you can find recorded documents, download free copies and order certified ones. It is the quickest way to confirm a deed or lien before you list. For land that moved to Broomfield in 2001, older records may sit in Boulder County.

Besides warranty deeds and quit claim deeds, the recorder accepts plats, military records and court documents such as letters and personal representative deeds. An estate sale can therefore be recorded in the same office as an ordinary sale.

Do not mix up the two counters. The Treasurer takes payments in Longmont on Mondays and in Boulder on weekdays, but the Treasurer is a separate office from the recorder. A tax payoff goes to the Treasurer at 303-441-3520, and a deed goes to the Clerk and Recorder at 303-413-7770.

sections.h2: Recording on closing day, step by step
sections.html:
For most sales, the title company handles recording and you never visit the office. If you are handling it yourself, the sequence is simple. Sign the deed, confirm the legal description with your title or legal help, and strip out personal identifying information. Calculate the fee: $43 for the document, plus the documentary fee if the price is over $500. Write the check to Boulder County Clerk & Recorder, add a return address, and choose a route: counter, drop box, mail or, for individual owners, a scanned PDF by email.

Plan around the office hours. With the counter closed Fridays, a deed signed on a Thursday afternoon has little room to spare, while the drop boxes accept filings around the clock. If you use the Lafayette or Longmont box, add the one to two business days that interoffice mail takes. When the document comes back, file it with your closing papers.

A cash sale follows the same steps. What it skips is the lender's deed of trust, so there is one fewer document to record, and there is no loan funding to wait on once the deed is filed.

sections.h2: Common situations for Boulder County sellers
sections.html:
Sellers here deal with high values, mixed ownership and mountain weather. A few situations come up again and again.

  • Estates and inherited houses, where court documents may need recording.
  • Rentals with tenants, and licensing steps that change when ownership changes.
  • Back property tax, which the title company pays out of proceeds.
  • Houses in areas hit by the 2013 floods or the Marshall Fire of December 30, 2021, where the history is part of the buyer's questions. A deed for a fire-damaged lot is recorded the same way as any other, and the same fees apply.

Before closing, make sure you have a plan for each one. Ask the title company who will record, when, and in which office, and keep the recorded deed when it comes back.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to record a deed in Boulder County?
faqs.a: The recording fee is $43 per document as of July 1, 2025. If the price is over $500, add the state documentary fee of one cent per $100 of consideration.

faqs.q: Is the Boulder County recorder open on Fridays?
faqs.a: No. The office is open Monday through Thursday from 7:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. and is closed Fridays. The three 24-hour drop boxes stay available.

faqs.q: Does Colorado charge a transfer tax on a house sale?
faqs.a: Colorado charges a documentary fee on deeds, not a separate transfer tax. It is one cent per $100 of consideration over $500, collected when the deed is recorded.

faqs.q: Can I e-record my own deed in Boulder County?
faqs.a: Individual owners can email a scanned PDF for a fee. E-recording through Simplifile, eRecording Partners, CSC or Indecomm is meant for high-volume filers such as title companies.

faqs.q: Where can I find an old Boulder County deed?
faqs.a: Use the county's public search site to find recorded documents, download free copies and order certified copies for $1. Land that moved to Broomfield in 2001 may have older records here.
